tour.title: Project Overview and Entry Points
tour.description: Curam Vault is an invite-based, multi-user AI workspace: one Node.js/Express server and one React 18/Vite frontend shipped together. server/index.js is the backend entry point and the most connected file in the graph: it sets up security middleware, logging and body parsers, mounts every public and authenticated API router plus the built SPA, then initialises the database schema and starts the cron jobs. On the client, main.jsx mounts App.jsx, which wires auth-guarded and feature-gated routes for every workspace page, and package.json ties both halves together with the dev/build/start scripts and the Anthropic, Gemini, Express and pg dependencies.

tour.title: The Database Foundation
tour.description: server/db.js holds the PostgreSQL connection pool with traced query logging and a single initSchema that creates and migrates every table, index and seed row in the application. It is the most depended-upon server file, so nearly every router and service you meet later reads and writes through it. db.js runs initSchema by itself the first time it is required (index.js from Step 1 just waits until the users table exists), so the schema code runs on every boot and has to be idempotent.
tour.languageLesson: Idempotent SQL DDL uses forms like CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS and ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS, so the same script can run on every boot against a fresh or an existing database without failing.

tour.title: Authentication and Request Context
tour.description: Before any /api router runs, the auth middleware looks up the bearer token in the auth_sessions table and offers guards for admin-only routes and for feature-access flags (including accountant access), so each tool can be turned on or off per member. requestContext.js tags every log line in a request with a requestId and userId, which is how activity gets traced across a multi-user server. Together they form the gate that index.js puts in front of the authenticated routers.
tour.languageLesson: Node's AsyncLocalStorage (from async_hooks) keeps a per-request store that follows a request through awaits and callbacks, so deep code can read the current requestId without passing it through every function.

tour.title: Client API Bridge and State
tour.description: apiClient.js is the most imported file in the whole project: every page calls the /api endpoints through it. It attaches the bearer token held in the persisted Zustand authStore, sends the user back to login on a 401, and handles downloads. Feedback goes through toastStore, a small Zustand store for transient notifications, so the pages stay free of HTTP and auth plumbing.
tour.languageLesson: Zustand stores are hooks created with create((set) => ({...})). Components subscribe to just the slices they need, and the persist middleware saves the state to localStorage so the auth token survives a page reload.

tour.title: The App Shell and Icons
tour.description: Every tool page renders inside Layout.jsx, which provides the top bar, sidebar, mobile navigation, toasts, reminders and digest popups, and loads settings plus the user's feature access. featureAccess.js holds the defaults and labels for the per-member toggles enforced on the server in Step 3. IconProvider exposes a useIcon hook that maps semantic icon names to the selected icon pack, which is why it is imported by hundreds of components.
tour.languageLesson: React Context plus a custom hook (useIcon) lets any component deep in the tree read shared configuration without passing props down manually. Changing the provider's value re-renders the components that consume it.

tour.title: Anatomy of a Tool: Notes
tour.description: Each Vault tool pairs a page under client/src/pages with a router under server/routes, and Notes is a good example to read first. NotesPage.jsx is the workspace UI, with serialized autosave, tags, templates, saved views, voice notes, AI actions and version history, and it lazy-loads the rich Tiptap editor. It talks through apiClient (Step 4) to routes/notes.js, which covers listing, AI ask, versions, reminders and recycle-bin deletes behind the auth gate from Step 3. Once you know this pattern, the other pages and routers follow the same shape.
tour.languageLesson: React.lazy(() => import('./Editor')) plus <Suspense> splits a heavy component into its own bundle chunk that only downloads the first time it renders.

tour.title: Calling AI Models
tour.description: AI features do not call provider SDKs directly. modelResolver.js decides which models a user may use, validating the models catalogue from settings and picking light, standard or heavy tiers. callModel.js then routes the call to Anthropic, DeepSeek, Gemini or local Ollama based on the model id prefix. logUsage.js records token usage and cost per user, session and feature, so every AI call can be accounted for. All three sit near the top of the server's fan-in ranking.

tour.title: Embeddings, Memory and Retrieval
tour.description: For meaning-based search, embeddings.js turns text into vectors through Gemini or Ollama and fetches the closest pgvector chunks for retrieval-augmented generation. MemoryService.js stores deduplicated per-user memories as 768-dimension vectors in pgvector. noteAsk.js powers 'ask your notes' from Step 6: a light model (chosen as in Step 7) plans the search, and the results combine Postgres full-text and embedding rankings.
tour.languageLesson: pgvector adds a vector column type and distance operators such as <=> (cosine distance) to PostgreSQL, so a nearest-neighbour search is just ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT k.

tour.title: Per-Page AI Guides
tour.description: Every tool page has a guide chat built from the same parts. On the server, guideCore.js is the shared engine: it builds the prompt from a page's catalogue of real controls, its rules and its list of unsupported actions, calls the workspace model, and normalises a verdict-style JSON reply. services/notesTutor.js supplies that catalogue for Notes, and makeGuideRouter in guideRouter.js turns it into an endpoint. On the client, TutorChat.jsx is the shared draggable chat, wrapped in an error boundary so a failing guide never breaks its page.

tour.title: Larger Tool Modules
tour.description: Bigger tools keep their logic in service sub-packages instead of in routers. Contract Review is a typical one: contractService.js handles CRUD with access control, corrections and obligation tracking, while analysisPipeline.js runs the multi-stage analysis (type detection, parties, clause classification, risk scoring, obligations) and pauses to ask the user to confirm party roles. Cross-cutting services such as the recycle bin are shared too: tools call moveToBin when something is deleted, and registered adapters restore it within 30 days.

tour.title: Scheduled Background Jobs
tour.description: index.js also starts the node-cron jobs that run periodic syncs, digests and cleanups. recurringCron.js, for example, creates the recurring finance transactions and invoices used by the Finance router, and finance.js is one of the largest routers, with about 113 endpoints. cronLock.js uses a Postgres advisory lock so that during a rolling deploy two containers do not run the same job twice.
tour.languageLesson: pg_try_advisory_lock(key) returns true only to the first session that asks for that key, which makes it a lightweight distributed mutex that needs no extra infrastructure beyond the database.

tour.title: Build and Deployment
tour.description: The whole app ships as one container on Railway. Dockerfile.base installs the slow, rarely changing layers: Node 20, LibreOffice, ffmpeg, poppler, Python dependencies and Playwright Chromium. The thin Dockerfile builds on that image, copies the code, runs the Vite builds and starts server/index.js on port 3000. railway.toml sets the build and start commands, the /api/health check and the restart policy, and nixpacks.toml adds system packages for builds that use Nixpacks.
tour.languageLesson: Splitting a heavy base image from a thin app image is like a multi-stage build spread over two Dockerfiles: system packages are built once and reused, so a code change only rebuilds the small top layers.
